chapter: Trombone technique, plunger mute and the California years
title: Growing up in a small segregated town with few records and no radio
summary: He was born in 1906 in a town of 10,000 with 500 black residents, heard few records and visiting bands, and envies the exposure kids have today.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Well, New Orleans just probably had a more opportunities for musicians because there was so much music there.

Yeah, New Orleans is a big town. I came from a little town, you know. I came from a small town -- 10,000 people. And it was a sort of segregated town, too, in that part, too, so there was only five hundred Colored people there. You know? So where am I going to play? That's when... I was born... I mean, when I was a kid... 1906, that's a long while ago, you know. And so the country wasn't completely settled good yet. You know?
Also you didn't have... The phonograph had just about come on the scene.

Phonographs had just come out, and only people with a lot of money could afford one. And you'd get a record... A record would come out about once or twice a year, a new record. So you'd play that one record you got

all year long. You know what I mean? Like today, the kids have such a chance. You know, if I could have heard the things that the kids can hear now... See, they got radio and they got television. They can see you doing it. You know what I mean? There was a difference than when I came along, because I had never seen nobody doin' nothin', you know. Now and then, a band would come through the town, so everybody would go to hear it. And I know I just to just love to hear bands. So that's the way that was.
They didn't have things like street parades and so on.

Now and then, a minstrel show would come in town, and they'd make a parade up the street, you know, and they'd play the pieces, like the Scott Joplin numbers. You know what I mean? [SINGS A REFRAIN] Them things. Heh-heh.
Well, there's a tremendous difference now, with kids being exposed to stuff.

Sure. Kids have got such a chance to hear anything. Boy, when I came along, what t would I give for this. Hmm-hmm-hmm! It's like they say, I was born fifty years too soon. But I'm happy to be born fifty years sooner than these kids, and I wish I could stay and see the whole thing through. Which is about, oh, a hundred million more years. [LAUGHS]
On the other hand, maybe the way you grew up and you more or less had to invent your own way....
And then today, maybe it's too easy, and kids don't know who to sound like. In a way, there's too many things pulling at you.
Yeah. You got problems all right. [LAUGHS]
